newsitem.title: LEBANON: Casino du Liban, pre-war highlife symbol, reopens.
newsitem.headline: Casino du Liban, pre-war highlife symbol, reopens.

text.p: Dice will roll again on Wednesday in the famed Casino du Liban, which is betting a $50 million facelift can restore its former glory as the Middle East's most famous gambling and entertainment centre before civil war broke out in 1975 and forced the casino to close.
President Elias Hrawi, in a ceremony on Tuesday night attended by VIPs, inaugurated the lavishly-refurbished casino overlooking the picturesque Bay of Jounieh north of Beirut.

Twelve months of restoration work wiped away the bullet and shell scars from fighting between militias, and now expensive Italian marble covers the exterior of the hilltop casino. Inside, huge crystal chandeliers hang from the ceiling.

The announcement of the casino's reopening has caused a sensation in Beirut. The local media reminisced over its pre-war world famous floor shows that drew the European and Arab jet-set and were a symbol of Lebanon's highlife then.
"No two people disagree that Lebanon lived the big days of glory in the sixties and seventies. The casino was one of those facets of glory," wrote the leading daily an-Nahar on Monday.
"We are full of hope the 'Pearl of the East' (casino) will again shine in the fields of art, tourism and entertainment."

U.S. vice president Lyndon Johnson and Arab kings, princes and presidents were among VIPs who enjoyed the casino's world-famous pre-war floor shows like "La Parisienne" and "Mais Oui" that featured dancing girls, Cossacks, elephants and dolphins.
The casino, inaugurated in January 1959, also hosted the Miss Europe pageant from 1960 to 1965.

Under the first phase of the re-opening, gambling halls with 60 new tables and 318 slot machines were refurbished, along with five of its seven restaurants. The Baccarat nightclub, whose pre-war predecessor was dubbed by the international press as one of the world's best, was also restored.
Next summmer will witness the opening of a 1,200-seat theatre and the famed "Salle des Ambassadeurs" where dance, magic, three-dimensional image and laser shows will be staged.
A 150-room luxury hotel will be opened by the year 2000.
The Compagnie du Casino du Liban has won a 30-year concession from the government to run the casino. London Club International will be in charge of gaming while Albert Abella will handle catering.
Nicholas Crabtree, the casino's British vice president of gaming, has said that he expects the casino to match, if not top, its prewar glory.
"The Middle East is an attractive market," Crabtree, of London Club International, said recently.

"There's a lot of customers who wish to gamble. A lot of those customers go to London and Monte Carlo and a few others go to America and other places. But to have a casino in their homeland, here in Lebanon, must be attractive," he said.
"It will be very, very popular, I'm sure," he said.
